prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a new tool that opens a door: the twist angle becomes a tuning knob for strongly correlated physics in a single van der Waals material, and the moire field grew out of it. The structure matches what the prize is for. There is a specific prediction (the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of flat bands at the magic angle) and an original, experimentally verified discovery (the 2018 correlated insulator and superconductivity experiments from Jarillo-Herrero's group). Seven of eight of us ranked it, five within the top five, and the three credited names were proposed nearly unanimously, which is rare. The basic phase diagram has been reproduced by many independent groups, and the discovery is already felt in materials and device physics. The unsettled pairing mechanism is a question about what comes after the door is open. It does not undermine the discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Earlier flat-band work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto is not in the credited names, and the 2018 experiment was carried out by a team in which the first-author students, Cao and others, did the hands-on work. A prize naming Jarillo-Herrero alone on the experimental side leaves the record open to criticism. A second concern is that the pairing mechanism, sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder and the nature of the correlated states are still debated, so some will call recognition early. Finally, the competing optical lattice clock candidate (B049) has the larger first-place support, and a purist could say the moire result is still moving fast while the clock is settled and mature.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a textbook measurement advance, with Katori's magic-wavelength idea followed by Ye's record accuracy, and a clean two-person configuration with credit that appears reasonably settled.
responses.response: I agree that the clock is verified, mature and cleanly attributed, and it is my own second choice, which is why I name it as the first alternative. Where I differ is on novelty. You yourself note that Ye's frequency-comb and laser-stabilisation work sits partly in territory honoured in 2005, and the ion clocks were honoured in 2012. I would ask whether the lattice clock is a new door or a much better version of a door already opened. I read it as an extraordinary refinement of an honoured lineage, whereas twisted bilayer graphene created a regime nobody could previously access. I would still be comfortable if the committee found a clear original-experiment argument for Katori, and I would like the historical record on who first demonstrated lattice clocks checked before we dismiss it.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the moire candidate fourth. He accepts the 2011 prediction and the 2018 discovery as a sensible theory-plus-experiment pairing, but flags the earlier flat-band work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, the experimental co-first authors, and the possibility that the fractional Chern insulator is the more stable result to award later.
responses.response: Your attribution point is the one I take most seriously, and I do not think it can be dismissed. My answer is that the Lopes dos Santos work found a reduced Fermi velocity at small angles, while the Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation predicted the flat bands at specific magic angles, which is the part the experiment then tested. I would want the committee to check this against the primary literature rather than rely on any of our memories. On the fractional Chern insulator, I think it argues for patience on a later prize, not for withholding this one. The 2018 correlated insulator and superconductivity experiments are the original ones, and a later, more elegant result should not displace them. I do agree that the superconductivity claim is the least settled part, so a citation that names the correlated states carefully is wiser than one resting on the pairing mechanism.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the moire candidate first for the same theory-to-experiment link, but asks whether the third credited name, Bistritzer, is needed for a fair configuration.
responses.response: I think the third name is needed. The 2011 paper was written by Bistritzer and MacDonald together, and removing Bistritzer would mean splitting a single result. If we are going to credit the prediction at all, I do not see a principled basis for crediting only one author. If the committee wants to leave a seat for the experiment, the harder question is whether Cao, who did the hands-on 2018 work, has a claim stronger than Bistritzer's. The prize rules limit us to three, and the supplied names were proposed almost unanimously, so I keep the trio. I would want that choice revisited if the historical record turns up a clear priority problem.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the clock first for its clean quantum-experiment character and the 1e-18 precision, and raises circuit QED second while flagging his own proximity to those groups.
responses.response: I value the clock for the same reason you do, and I appreciate your open statement about circuit QED. On B040, I would add that the 2025 prize in superconducting circuits makes another award in the area a hard sell this year, and Girvin's absence from the credited names is a real attribution gap. I also share your uncertainty whether the committee will see the clock as a distinct discovery or an extension of 2005 and 2012. Since you are at Chalmers and I am too, I will say plainly that this is not a point of difference between us on science. It is a judgment on novelty, and I would rather the committee settle it on the record than on our shared preferences.

uncertainties: Whether earlier flat-band theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and the experimental co-first authors (Cao and others) are given enough weight by a Bistritzer-MacDonald-Jarillo-Herrero trio. I have not verified the primary literature.
Whether the pairing mechanism remains too open for a citation that names superconductivity, or whether the correlated insulator discovery is the safer anchor.
Whether the lattice clock should be treated as a distinct invention or an extension of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, and who first demonstrated the lattice clock.
Whether a two-part prize is warranted. A combined configuration cannot exceed three people, which makes pairing the moire candidate with the clock impractical.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the moire candidate from my profile. I have no known collaboration with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer. General connections I should flag are that Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague and that Mehlig is in the neighbouring GU department, and that Chalmers has superconducting-circuit activity relevant to B040, which I do not prefer.
